Templates: plan-*

Node types: plan-doc, plan-task, plan-step, plan-check — four templates, one file, nested three deep, per the family-file convention
File naming: this file is plan.template.html, named after the plan-* family it defines. Documents that conform to plan-doc are named <date>-<topic>.plan.html
Purpose: the shape an implementation plan takes when written as a v4 node instead of the superpowers:writing-plans skill's default Markdown — the same override spec.template.html already made for superpowers:brainstorming's spec output
Sibling of: knowledge.template.html, spec.template.html
Styling: ./plan.template.css, this family's own rendering rules, plus the shared ../theme.css every document links

Four nested conforming types, not one flat schema

plan-doc contains plan-tasks, each independently conforming to #plan-task; plan-task contains plan-steps, each conforming to #plan-step; plan-step contains at most one plan-check, conforming to #plan-check. This is the same pattern spec.template.html's own "Conformance" section documents: a document can have any number of typed elements nested inside it, each independently addressable via its own data-conforms-to. A parent's own <template> only ever declares a nested child tag as "may be present" — it can't reach into that child's own internal shape, which is why each of the three nested types needs its own data-conforms-to: pnpm mycelium validate's crawler finds every validatable instance purely by scanning for [data-conforms-to] anywhere in the tree.

plan-title repeats across all three nesting levels (doc, task, step) — fields belong to the family, not to one type within it, same as every other family here. This is exactly the scenario that required fixing template.template.html's generic validator to scope its field lookups to direct children only, rather than searching an instance's entire subtree.

The four types

plan-doc

Fields: title, date, goal, architecture, optional tech-stack, optional global-constraints, optional (repeatable) plan-task children. No stored status — it is derived from the tasks, which derive from their steps. The optional status field accepts only rejected.

<plan-doc data-conforms-to="./plan.template.html#plan-doc">
  <plan-title>…</plan-title>
  <plan-date>2026-07-25</plan-date>
  <plan-goal>…</plan-goal>
  <plan-architecture>…</plan-architecture>
</plan-doc>

plan-task

Fields: title, files, optional interfaces, optional (repeatable) plan-step children. No stored status — all steps completed is completed, some is active, none is pending. The optional status field accepts only rejected, which no arrangement of steps can imply.

<plan-task id="task-1" data-conforms-to="./plan.template.html#plan-task">
  <plan-title>…</plan-title>
  <plan-files>Create: …</plan-files>
</plan-task>

plan-step

Fields: title, status (pending|completed — a single step is only ever done or not), optional detail, optional plan-check child. This is the only level where status is stored: it is the layer everything above folds from, and check sets it from a real command's exit code rather than from anyone's memory.

<plan-step id="task-1-step-1" data-conforms-to="./plan.template.html#plan-step">
  <plan-title>Write the failing test</plan-title>
  <plan-status>pending</plan-status>
</plan-step>

plan-check

Fields: command, optional success (enum true|false, code default "true" when absent), optional output (a plain substring match).

<plan-check data-conforms-to="./plan.template.html#plan-check">
  <plan-check-command>pytest tests/foo.py::test_bar -v</plan-check-command>
  <plan-check-success>false</plan-check-success>
  <plan-check-output>function not defined</plan-check-output>
</plan-check>

A worked example

One realistic nested instance: a doc containing a task containing a step containing a check. Each of the four carries its own data-conforms-to, so each is checked separately against the type it names, which is what makes this a worked example of the nesting rather than of one type.

They are real instances, not illustrations. mycelium validate finds them the same way it finds every instance in the corpus and checks them with the shared validateFromTemplate, so this file fails if one stops conforming.

Sample plan 2026-07-25 Build the thing. Do it in a few small steps. Sample task Create: src/thing.ts Sample step pending echo ok true

Authoring commands

add and update each take a kind (doc, task, or step) as their own first positional argument and dispatch internally — the same convention knowledge add <type> already established, reused here instead of four separate hyphenated command names, which JavaScript can't export as plain identifiers.

check shells out to a step's plan-check-command (or every step's, if the caller omits a step id), compares the exit code against plan-check-success and, if present, substring-matches plan-check-output against combined stdout/stderr. A pass flips that step's plan-status to completed; a fail leaves it untouched and the command exits nonzero once every step has been tried. Steps with no plan-check are skipped, not treated as failures.

list is read-only: one line per plan-step (its task's id/title, its own id/title, status, and whether it has a plan-check), reporting whatever's already on disk rather than re-running anything — a flat progress view over a plan-doc's nested tasks/steps.
